findings.claim: Of the 300 ships that had carried the Norwegian army to England, reportedly only 25 returned.
findings.truth: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records 24 ships, not 25, as enough to carry the survivors home.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Stamford Bridge': 'only 24 ships from the fleet of over 300 were needed to carry the survivors away'.

findings.claim: The subsequent Treaty of Wedmore established the Danelaw.
findings.truth: 'Treaty of Wedmore' is a modern label for the 878 settlement at which Guthrum was baptised; the Danelaw boundary was set by the later Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum. The usage is standard in GCSE textbooks, so no edit.
findings.evidence: general Anglo-Saxon scholarship; standard textbook usage

findings.claim: John lost Normandy to France at the Battle of Bouvines (1214).
findings.truth: John lost Normandy in 1204, when Philip II conquered it. Bouvines (July 1214) was the defeat of John's allies that ended his attempt to win Normandy back. The lesson gives an effect as the cause and is ten years out.
findings.evidence: standard Angevin chronology (fall of Rouen, June 1204; Bouvines, 27 July 1214)

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: "King John's arbitrary taxation and loss of Normandy at Bouvines (1214) turned barons against him".
findings.truth: Same error as F3. Normandy was lost in 1204.
findings.evidence: standard Angevin chronology

findings.claim: Chronicler Orderic Vitalis ... described the land lying uncultivated for nine years and thousands of bodies left to rot.
findings.truth: The 'nine years' waste claim is not Orderic's; it belongs to the Durham tradition. Orderic's own recorded claim is that more than 100,000 people perished of starvation. Attribution corrected to what Orderic wrote.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Harrying of the North', quoting Orderic Vitalis: 'More than 100,000 people perished of starvation.'

findings.claim: the regent William Marshal defeated the French at the Battle of Lincoln (1217), ending the war
findings.truth: Lincoln (May 1217) was decisive but the war ended after the naval battle off Sandwich (August 1217) and the Treaty of Lambeth (September 1217). The compression is normal at GCSE, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard First Barons' War chronology

findings.claim: Glossary: 'chevauchée — The negative effects of armies moving through an area, including destruction of crops, livestock and property and the spread of disease.'
findings.truth: A chevauchée is the raid itself — a fast mounted raid to burn and plunder enemy land — not the effects of armies passing through. The lesson's own knowledge check defines it correctly, so the glossary and the in-text definition contradict the question a student is marked on.
findings.evidence: standard Hundred Years' War military vocabulary; the lesson's own knowledge check 3

findings.claim: In-text <dfn> for Chevauchée carries the same wrong definition as the glossary.
findings.truth: Same as F7 — the pop-up definition must match the raid, not the effects.
findings.evidence: standard Hundred Years' War military vocabulary

findings.claim: Edward I intervened in a succession dispute in 1296, deposed the Scottish king John Balliol and declared himself overlord.
findings.truth: Edward judged the disputed succession (the Great Cause) in 1291–92 and awarded the throne to Balliol. He invaded and deposed Balliol in 1296. The lesson collapses two separate events five years apart into one.
findings.evidence: standard Scottish Wars of Independence chronology

findings.claim: Between 1277 and 1283, Edward I ... building a network of concentric stone castles — Caernarfon, Harlech, Conwy, Beaumaris.
findings.truth: Beaumaris was not begun until 1295, after the revolt the lesson mentions in the next clause, so it cannot belong to 1277–83. Caernarfon and Conwy are walled enclosure castles, not concentric ones.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the Welsh castles (Beaumaris begun 1295)

findings.claim: Takeaway: 'his Scottish campaigns (1296–1328) ultimately failed'.
findings.truth: Edward I died in 1307, so his campaigns cannot run to 1328. The lesson's own key fact gives 1296–1307. 1328 is the treaty that ended the wider war.
findings.evidence: Edward I died 7 July 1307; the lesson's own key fact

findings.claim: At Gravelines, English fireships sent into the anchored fleet caused panic and dispersal.
findings.truth: The fireships were sent into the Armada anchored off Calais on the night of 7–8 August. The Spanish cut their cables and scattered; the battle of Gravelines was fought the next day against the scattered ships. The lesson merges two separate events that students are routinely asked to distinguish.
findings.evidence: standard Armada chronology (Calais fireships 7-8 August; Gravelines 8 August 1588)

findings.claim: Knowledge check 2 asks what tactic the English used 'at Gravelines' and keys 'Fireships sent into the anchored Spanish fleet'.
findings.truth: Same error as F12 — the fireships were used off Calais, so the keyed answer only becomes right once the stem is corrected.
findings.evidence: standard Armada chronology

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'What tactic disrupted the Armada at Gravelines?'
findings.truth: Same error as F12 — the fireships were sent in off Calais.
findings.evidence: standard Armada chronology

findings.claim: storms wrecked perhaps two-thirds of the fleet. Around 50 ships and perhaps 15,000 Spanish sailors and soldiers died.
findings.truth: The two figures contradict each other: 50 of 130 ships is under 40 per cent, not two-thirds. About half the fleet came home. Losses were also not all from storms.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; standard Armada loss figures (about 130 sailed, roughly 60-67 returned)

findings.claim: Mark note for question 2 tells students 'Atlantic storms wrecked two-thirds of the Armada' and dates the fireships to Gravelines.
findings.truth: Both facts are corrected by F12 and F15; a mark note that rewards the wrong version would cost marks.
findings.evidence: standard Armada chronology and loss figures

findings.claim: it generated its own legal term: 'blackmail' ... and the phrase 'bereaved' (to have been raided and robbed)
findings.truth: 'Blackmail' does come from border protection payments. 'Bereaved' does not: it comes from Old English bereafian, to rob or deprive, centuries before the reivers, and it never meant 'raided'. This is an invented etymology and is removed.
findings.evidence: Old English bereafian; standard etymology

findings.claim: Henry VIII's Italian wars, for example, were accompanied by Scottish raiding that culminated at Flodden (1513).
findings.truth: Henry VIII fought in France in 1513 (Thérouanne and Tournai), not Italy, and James IV invaded England rather than merely raiding. Calling it an 'Italian war' would mislead a student badly.
findings.evidence: Henry VIII's French campaign of 1513; Flodden 9 September 1513

findings.claim: The Armstrong clan ... Hundreds were executed or transported to Ireland in the early seventeenth century.
findings.truth: The mass transportation to Ireland in 1606 was of the Grahams, not the Armstrongs; the Armstrongs were broken mainly by hangings. The lesson gives one family another's fate.
findings.evidence: the Graham transportation to Roscommon, 1606; the pacification of the Middle Shires

findings.claim: Examiners reward students who explain why the change happened when it did, not just that it happened.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. No board publishes this. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Estimates of military deaths in England alone range from 85,000 to 200,000; deaths from disease ... added further to the toll.
findings.truth: The upper figure of about 200,000 already includes deaths from disease, so adding disease deaths on top double-counts. The range itself is defensible, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard English Civil War casualty estimates (about 85,000 killed in action, about 100,000 from disease)

findings.claim: James Francis Edward Stuart ('the Old Pretender') launched a rising in Scotland and northern England.
findings.truth: The Earl of Mar raised the standard at Braemar in September 1715 in James's name. James himself did not reach Scotland until December, as the lesson's own next sentence says.
findings.evidence: standard 1715 chronology; the lesson's own following sentence

findings.claim: The rising was crushed at Sheriffmuir.
findings.truth: Sheriffmuir (13 November 1715) was a drawn battle. Mar held the larger army and failed to win, which stalled the rising; the Jacobite force in England surrendered at Preston the next day.
findings.evidence: standard 1715 chronology (Sheriffmuir indecisive; Preston surrender 14 November 1715)

findings.claim: Only Charles's decision to retreat north (against his own preference) prevented a direct march on the capital.
findings.truth: This contradicts itself and the lesson's own key fact. The retreat was voted by Charles's council of war, led by Lord George Murray, against Charles's wishes.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own key fact; standard account of the Derby council of war, 5-6 December 1745

findings.claim: with Liberal politician Emily Hobhouse's reports causing public outrage
findings.truth: Emily Hobhouse was a welfare campaigner, not a politician. She never held office or stood for Parliament.
findings.evidence: Emily Hobhouse, South African Women and Children Distress Fund; standard biography

findings.claim: Examiners reward students who push beyond description to analyse the relationship between war and social or political change.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners reward. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: At Peterloo ... killing fifteen and injuring hundreds (also 'Fifteen people died' in the collapsible, a knowledge check option and a flashcard).
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. Fifteen is the traditional count and the figure on the Manchester red plaque; current research (Michael Bush) and Wikipedia's lead give eighteen, and the true total was never officially established. The ripple is four places including a keyed knowledge check option. My recommendation: leave the figure but soften the two prose mentions to 'at least fifteen', and leave the knowledge check and flashcard alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Peterloo Massacre': lead states eighteen killed, the red plaque states fifteen, and the article notes 'the exact number ... has never been established with certainty'
findings.ruling: Leave: fifteen is the traditional plaque figure; eighteen is a research revision.

findings.claim: Trafalgar ended the threat of a French invasion of Britain.
findings.truth: Napoleon had already broken up the Army of England and marched east in August 1805, two months before Trafalgar. The claim is standard in textbooks, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard Napoleonic chronology (Grande Armée leaves Boulogne, August 1805)

findings.claim: she reduced mortality rates dramatically through improved sanitation and hygiene [at Scutari]
findings.truth: Mortality at Scutari rose during Nightingale's first months and fell after the Sanitary Commission rebuilt the sewers in March 1855; Nightingale herself later accepted this. The lesson gives the standard account, which a mark scheme would credit, so no edit.
findings.evidence: standard revisionist scholarship on Scutari mortality

findings.claim: women aged 19–30 were conscripted for war work or the auxiliary services from 1941
findings.truth: The National Service (No. 2) Act of December 1941 made unmarried women aged 20–30 liable. The age range was widened later; 19 is not the starting age.
findings.evidence: National Service (No. 2) Act 1941

findings.claim: Around 1.4 million children were evacuated from cities.
findings.truth: About 1.5 million people were evacuated under the September 1939 government scheme, of whom about 827,000 were unaccompanied schoolchildren; the rest were mothers with infants, teachers and helpers. The lesson turns the whole total into children.
findings.evidence: Operation Pied Piper, September 1939: about 1.5 million evacuated, 827,000 schoolchildren

findings.claim: Mark note for question 2 repeats 'around 1.4 million children were evacuated from cities'.
findings.truth: Same error as F31; a mark note must not reward the wrong figure.
findings.evidence: Operation Pied Piper figures

findings.claim: DORA ... clocks were moved to British Summer Time to maximise working hours
findings.truth: British Summer Time was created by the Summer Time Act 1916, not by DORA, though both were wartime measures. The grouping is common in GCSE resources, so no edit.
findings.evidence: Summer Time Act 1916

findings.claim: British paratroopers shot dead fourteen civilian marchers ... A further person died later from injuries.
findings.truth: Thirteen people were shot dead on the day. A fourteenth, John Johnston, died later from his injuries. The lesson as written adds up to fifteen deaths and would cost a student marks on the single most tested figure in this topic.
findings.evidence: standard Bloody Sunday record; Saville Inquiry

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: '30 January 1972 — British paratroopers shot dead 14 civilian marchers in Derry/Londonderry'.
findings.truth: Same error as F34: thirteen were shot dead on the day and a fourteenth died later.
findings.evidence: standard Bloody Sunday record

findings.claim: Britain's deployment in Afghanistan (2001–14) and Iraq (2003–09) ... resulted in 179 and 456 British military deaths respectively.
findings.truth: The two figures are the wrong way round. 179 British service personnel died in Iraq; about 456 died in Afghanistan. The sentence also claims these were the most sustained commitments since 1982, which ignores Operation Banner in Northern Ireland (1969–2007), described earlier in the same lesson.
findings.evidence: Ministry of Defence operational death tolls: Iraq 179, Afghanistan 457

findings.claim: The 7 July 2005 London bombings were carried out by four British-born men.
findings.truth: Three of the four were born in Britain. Germaine Lindsay was born in Jamaica and grew up in Britain.
findings.evidence: standard 7 July 2005 bombings record

findings.claim: examiners expect you to cite authoritative conclusions, not just describe events
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners expect. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

summary: Every lesson carried a practice set labelled in another board's question forms and tariffs (2/4/10/8 mark 'Describe One Feature', 'Describe Two Features', 'Explain Why', 'Explain Causation'); all ten sets are relabelled to the thematic study's four real forms (Describe 4, Explain 8, second order concept 14, essay 24). No lesson asserted a SPaG mark, paper or section, so nothing had to be unwound there. On content the serious errors were a transposed Iraq/Afghanistan death toll and a Bloody Sunday count that added up to fifteen deaths (L10), Normandy lost at Bouvines in 1214 rather than in 1204 (L2), and a chevauchee glossary definition that described the effects of war instead of the raid (L3). Lesson 6 was clean apart from the practice labels.
